<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-brassica" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-brassica-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of brassica vegetables, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

<a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach brassica vegetables

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

The evidence on how metals reach brassica vegetables comes from studies that compared exposed and ordinary settings. Brassica vegetables, as sold from Farm U1 (Urban), field samples had lead higher at 141 µg/kg, against 13.4 µg/kg for All six farms, field samples in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/kim2024-metals-kale-urban-rural-maryland|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Kim BF, Lupolt SN, Santo RE, Bachman G, Zhu X, Yang T, Fukagawa NK, Richardson ML, Green C, Phillips KM, Nachman KE · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/kim2024-metals-kale-urban-rural-maryland">Nutrients and non-essential metals in darkibor kale grown at urban and rural farms: a pilot study</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">PLOS ONE</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/kim2024-metals-kale-urban-rural-maryland">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In another study, brassica vegetables, as sold from urban vegetable farm irrigated with groundwater and (wastewater-irrigated fields) had total mercury higher at 3 µg/kg, against 1 µg/kg for urban vegetable farm irrigated with groundwater and in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/affum2020-sekondi-takoradi-urban-farm-vegetables-metals|9]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Affum AO, Osae SD, Kwaansa-Ansah EE, Miyittah MK · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/affum2020-sekondi-takoradi-urban-farm-vegetables-metals">Quality assessment and potential health risk of heavy metals in leafy and non-leafy vegetables irrigated with groundwater and municipal-waste-dominated stream in the Western Region, Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Heliyon 6 (2020) e05829</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/affum2020-sekondi-takoradi-urban-farm-vegetables-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> A third study found that brassica vegetables, as sold from local vendors, Dehradun City (wastewater-irrigated fields) had Cu higher at 940 µg/kg, against 370 µg/kg for walled garden control in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/chemistry2022-bio-accumulation-of-heavy-metals-in-some-north|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">INDIAN LEAFY VEGETABLES AND QUANTIFICATION OF CONSUMER HEALTH RISK DUE TO THEIR DIETARY INTAKE SHAIL KULSHRESTHA Department of Chemistry, D. B. S. (P. G.) College, Dehradun, India ( · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/chemistry2022-bio-accumulation-of-heavy-metals-in-some-north">BIO-ACCUMULATION OF HEAVY METALS IN SOME NORTH</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Peer-reviewed article</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/chemistry2022-bio-accumulation-of-heavy-metals-in-some-north">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

These are observational comparisons from single studies; the size of the difference depends on the site, metal and distance.



<a id="ranges-by-source-region-and-variety"></a>
## Which forms and regions measured lower

<a id="hmi-ing-013"></a>
<a id="how-do-concentrations-vary-by-origin-growing-conditions-variety-and-harvest-period"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-014"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-distinguishes-within-lot-between-lot-supplier-and-production-system-variation"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-015"></a>
<a id="which-comparisons-support-a-sourcing-decision-and-where-would-geographic-or-supplier-generalization-be-unjustified"></a>

The HMI reference for lead in brassica vegetables, as sold pools 60 subgroup units from 3 sampling families, with a median of 25 µg/kg and a middle half spanning between 7.88 and 10 (lower quartile) and 540 µg/kg (upper quartile).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span <details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-brassica-vegetables" data-anchor="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-brassica-vegetables" data-question="How do heavy metals get into brassica vegetables?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How do heavy metals get into brassica vegetables?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In the studies available, brassica vegetables from contaminated or exposed settings carried more metal than brassica vegetables from the same study’s control.<sup class="cite">[[sources/kim2024-metals-kale-urban-rural-maryland|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Kim BF, Lupolt SN, Santo RE, Bachman G, Zhu X, Yang T, Fukagawa NK, Richardson ML, Green C, Phillips KM, Nachman KE · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/kim2024-metals-kale-urban-rural-maryland">Nutrients and non-essential metals in darkibor kale grown at urban and rural farms: a pilot study</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">PLOS ONE</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/kim2024-metals-kale-urban-rural-maryland">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Brassica vegetables, as sold from Farm R3 (Rural), field samples had lead higher at 13.6 µg/kg, against 13.4 µg/kg for All six farms, field samples in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/kim2024-metals-kale-urban-rural-maryland|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Kim BF, Lupolt SN, Santo RE, Bachman G, Zhu X, Yang T, Fukagawa NK, Richardson ML, Green C, Phillips KM, Nachman KE · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/kim2024-metals-kale-urban-rural-maryland">Nutrients and non-essential metals in darkibor kale grown at urban and rural farms: a pilot study</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">PLOS ONE</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/kim2024-metals-kale-urban-rural-maryland">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-brassica-vegetables" data-anchor="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-brassica-vegetables" data-question="Which regions report the lowest levels in brassica vegetables?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which regions report the lowest levels in brassica vegetables?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Among GEMS/Food reporting regions, brassica vegetables, as sold had the lowest lead subgroup median in PAHO (5.2 µg/kg) and the highest in WPRO (98 µg/kg); reporting regions are markets, not growing areas.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-brassica-vegetables-is-inorganic" data-anchor="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-brassica-vegetables-is-inorganic" data-question="How much of the arsenic in brassica vegetables is inorganic?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How much of the arsenic in brassica vegetables is inorganic?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Inorganic arsenic, the more toxic form, was measured in 3 results from 2 sources, far fewer than total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs|12]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Dietary exposure to inorganic arsenic in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2014;12(3):3597</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) 2014 reported inorganic arsenic at 5.6 µg/kg (mean) in brassica vegetables, as sold from European dietary-survey occurrence data.<sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs|12]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Dietary exposure to inorganic arsenic in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2014;12(3):3597</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
